title: Mining of important genetic loci and evaluation of genetic effects for growth traits in Baicheng You Chicken.
authors: Jiang T, You G, Li H, Hou Z, Zhao X, Dong W, Liao H, Zhang S, Yin Z.
ai_summary:
Gene: TAPT1
Finding: A genome-wide association study in 1,535 Baicheng You Chickens identified 145 significant SNPs for growth traits and annotated 22 candidate genes, with TAPT1 among the key candidates.
Disease: Growth traits (body weight, keel length, chest girth, pelvic width, chest depth, shank length, chest width, body slanting length)

title: Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae modulates ciliary function and epithelial integrity in air-liquid interface porcine respiratory epithelial cells (ALI-PRECs).
authors: Castillo-Espinoza AF, Nelli RK, Mora-Díaz JC, Zhang D, Rauh R, Reddi BM, Saxena A, Twu N-C, Espin-Palazón R, Giménez-Lirola LG.
ai_summary: This study developed an air-liquid interface porcine respiratory epithelial cell (ALI-PREC) model from primary tracheal epithelial cells of three pigs to study Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (Mhp) infection, which causes enzootic pneumonia by disrupting mucociliary clearance. Mhp adhered within 2 hours and induced dose- and time-dependent cytopathic effects (cell rounding, clustering, detachment) and reduced ciliary activity, with bacterial DNA detected in the epithelium by 24 hpi and in subnatants at higher doses, indicating barrier disruption. Ciliary beating persisted in some replicates, revealing interindividual variability in host response. Gene expression analysis showed downregulation of ciliary motility genes (ROPN1L, LRRC51, CEP162, LRRC6) at 72 hpi and upregulation of intercellular junction genes (CLDN1, CDH1, CTNND1) by 120 hpi, suggesting a wound healing response. Friis medium had no detectable effect on the cells, validating the model, which the authors propose as a robust platform for studying Mhp host-pathogen interactions and therapeutic targets.

title: Activated Platelets Express GPI-Anchored Fibrocystin-L (PKHD1L1), from Granules, Absent or Deficient in Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria.
authors: Polgar J, Clemetson JM, Magnenat E, Wells TN, Röss H, Rochat S, Alberio LA, Clemetson KJ.
ai_summary:
Gene: PKHD1L1
Finding: Fibrocystin-L (PKHD1L1) is a ~500 kDa GPI-anchored receptor stored in platelet granules and expressed on the surface of activated platelets, and it is missing or deficient in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria; CD109 was likewise found to be a granule protein.
Disease: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

title: Bayesian Genome-Wide Association Study of Feed Efficiency Traits in Pigs.
authors: Faggion S, Bonfatti V, Bergamasco A, Carnier P.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
ai_summary: This Bayesian GWAS of feed efficiency traits in 201 pigs identified trait-associated SNPs for residual feed intake, feed conversion ratio, and average daily feed intake across multiple Sus scrofa chromosomes, confirming the polygenic architecture of these traits. A candidate gene search around these SNPs revealed 41 genes involved in diverse processes such as intestinal development, nutrient transport and absorption, metabolic homeostasis, energy sensing, and neurological regulation, which together formed a highly interconnected network. The findings underscore the complexity of feed efficiency and the interplay of multiple physiological, metabolic, and regulatory pathways.

title: Ciliary neurotrophic factor slows axonal transport of signalling endosomes.
authors: Rhymes ER, Fetkowitz C, Schiavo G, Sleigh JN, Tosolini AP.
ai_summary: Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) applied to distal axon terminals markedly slowed the in vivo retrograde transport of signalling endosomes in both fast and slow motor neurons of anaesthetised mice, whereas pro-BDNF, hepatocyte growth factor and neurturin had no detectable effect on transport dynamics. This demonstrates that neurotrophic factors selectively regulate signalling endosome transport in motor neurons, a finding relevant to developing muscle-targeted therapeutic strategies for restoring axonal transport in neurodegenerative disease, peripheral neuropathy and nerve injury.

title: Evidence for dual pathways of Tc1/mariner domestication in Drosophila.
authors: Guseva IO, Rezvykh AP, Zelentsova ES, Kulikova DA, Evgen'ev MB, Funikov SY.
ai_summary: This genomic screen of 43 drosophilid species identified five high-confidence, conserved genes domesticated from Tc1/mariner transposases, revealing two distinct co-option pathways: one retaining the DNA-binding module (CG4570, cag, toy, and a recently domesticated lineage-restricted gene in the Drosophila obscura group) and one retaining the catalytic domain (CG14478, which preserves a canonical DDE endonuclease fold). Co-expression network analysis linked these genes to diverse cellular roles—RNA/chromatin processes (CG14478), cell cycle/chromosome functions (CG4570), ciliary and nuclear functions (cag), and neuronal development (toy)—indicating that domestication spans a continuum from recent, lineage-specific events to ancient, conserved genes.

title: Identification of GCNT3 as a glycometabolism-associated biomarker in endometrial cancer.
authors: Ke D, Li W, Xu J, He X, Wang Y, Tan J, Sun Y.
ai_summary:
Gene: GCNT3
Finding: GCNT3 is upregulated in endometrial cancer and independently predicts improved overall and disease-free survival, associates with lower tumor grade, earlier stage, distinct immune infiltration, and lower predicted IC50 values for Afatinib and Selumetinib, with molecular docking supporting binding to these drugs.
Disease: Endometrial carcinoma

title: Diallyl sulfide pretreatment protects against DSS-induced colitis by reshaping the gut microbiota and enhancing microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism.
authors: Wan X, Wu Y, Sun Y, Liu Y, Jia G.
ai_summary:
Gene: STAT3
Finding: Diallyl sulfide pretreatment protects against DSS-induced colitis by reshaping the gut microbiota and increasing indole-producing tryptophan metabolites (IPA and IAld), an effect mediated at least in part through the AhR/IL-22/STAT3 pathway, as AhR blockade with CH223191 reduced colonic IL-22 and the p-STAT3/STAT3 ratio and diminished protection.
Disease: DSS-induced colitis

title: Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor in Skeletal Muscle of Older Adults and the Effects of Weight Loss and Aerobic Training.
authors: Ryan AS, Li G, Lynch C, Jaber SM, Bigman G.
ai_summary: Skeletal muscle CNTF mRNA was measured in 67 older adults and related to adiposity, glucose tolerance, and metabolic rate, with a subset then completing six months of weight loss (n = 21) or supervised aerobic training (n = 20). At baseline, muscle CNTF expression was inversely associated with resting metabolic rate, fat oxidation, and 3-h glucose and insulin AUCs, but not with BMI, percent body fat, or VO2max. Weight loss lowered body weight, fat mass, glucose and insulin AUCs, and basal muscle CNTF, while aerobic training raised VO2max and lowered fat mass without changing body weight, glucose/insulin AUCs, or basal CNTF. Insulin-stimulated CNTF expression rose after both interventions, and the change in glucose disposal (M) correlated positively with the change in insulin-stimulated CNTF, suggesting muscle CNTF is linked to glucose intolerance rather than body composition or fitness, and that gains in insulin sensitivity accompany increased muscle CNTF during hyperinsulinemia.

title: The multifaceted significance of phosphoinositides in endocytic trafficking.
authors: Xie C, Shi A.
ai_summary: This review covers how the seven phosphoinositide species, despite making up under 10% of membrane lipids, act as compartment-specific "lipid codes" governing endocytic trafficking, including endocytosis, endosomal sorting, degradation, recycling, and caveolin-mediated uptake, through the actions of specific kinases and phosphatases. It highlights how tools such as fluorescent biosensors, super-resolution microscopy, optogenetics, and synthetic biology have advanced understanding of phosphoinositide dynamics, and notes that perturbed phosphoinositide metabolism is linked to human diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, suggesting therapeutic targets. Future work should address spatiotemporal regulation, tissue-specific metabolism, synergy with other lipids, and systems biology approaches to connect basic cell biology with translational medicine.

title: Targeting subchondral osteoporosis in osteoarthritis: biomechanical crosstalk and the therapeutic rationale for inflammatory microenvironment remodeling.
authors: Han M, Han L, Zhang S, Tian L, Luo G, Lin K, Su H, Zhang J, Yang F, He M, Wei Q.
ai_summary: This review proposes a phenotype-dependent, bidirectional framework linking subchondral bone remodeling to osteoarthritis. Abnormal mechanical loading may initiate compartment-specific subchondral changes, while high-turnover bone loss can reduce trabecular competence and amplify stress concentration, whereas late-stage OA may instead show a low-turnover sclerotic phenotype. The authors integrate these macroscopic biomechanical factors with local osteoimmune processes—macrophage-state heterogeneity, Th17/Treg imbalance, senescence-associated secretory signaling, and bone-vascular coupling. They emphasize that current evidence supports biological links among bone remodeling, inflammatory signaling, and osteochondral crosstalk, but does not establish that anti-osteoporotic therapy reverses malalignment or consistently alters OA progression. Bone-targeting treatment is therefore framed as a hypothesis requiring turnover- and phenotype-stratified clinical evaluation, and the proposed time-window model is intended to guide future research rather than serve as treatment guidance.

title: TGF-β-producing tBregs are associated with poor survival rates in PTGS2-high cancers.
authors: Premkumar K, Ramu S, Jolly MK, Shankar BS.
ai_summary:
Gene: STAT3
Finding: Tumor-derived PGE2 drives the formation of TGF-β-producing tumor-evoked regulatory B cells (tBregs) via non-canonical EP4/STAT3 signaling involving JNK and NF-κB, and a Breg gene signature is elevated in PTGS2-high tumors and associated with poor patient survival.
Disease: PTGS2-high cancers (including fibrosarcoma)

title: ILC3s as central regulators of mucosal homeostasis and disease pathogenesis (Review).
authors: Zhang J, Bao L, Li J, Li X, Qiao L, Cui J, He X, Zhang M, Lu J, Zhang X, Dong J, Tao G, Feng Y, Tian YP, Zhao P, Tuo Y.
ai_summary: This review summarizes the biology of type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s), which arise from common lymphoid progenitors under RORγt control and differentiate into NCR+ ILC3s, NCR− ILC3s, and lymphoid tissue inducer cells. Through IL-22, IL-17, and GM-CSF, ILC3s maintain epithelial barrier integrity, antimicrobial defense, and lymphoid tissue development, with their activity governed by transcription factors, metabolism, neuroimmune signals, and the circadian clock. ILC3s engage in bidirectional crosstalk with gut microbiota, and depending on subset composition and tissue context, they can be protective or pathogenic. The authors propose a spatiotemporal-quantitative framework and three regulatory axes to explain disease-specific ILC3 responses, highlighting ILC3s as potential targets for precision immunotherapy in inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer.

title: Interplay between pathogen-mediated immune evasion and innate immune negative regulation in gastrointestinal tumors.
authors: Shi M, Zeng Y, Chen C, Zuo X.
ai_summary: This review argues that the key driver of pathogen-associated gastrointestinal cancer is not the intensity of chronic inflammation but an imbalance between sustained inflammatory stimulation and insufficient immune elimination. It examines how three functionally distinct layers converge: pathogen-mediated immune evasion (via virulence factors of H. pylori, EBV, F. nucleatum, ETBF, and pks-positive E. coli), host-derived innate immune negative regulation that dampens PRR- and interferon-associated signaling, and adaptive immune checkpoint suppression. Together these impair antigen presentation, cytotoxic responses, and pathogen clearance, fostering immune tolerance and tumor progression, and suggesting a conceptual basis for pathogen control, innate immune reprogramming, and precision therapy.

title: The Role of S100A8/A9 in Autoimmune Eye Diseases: From Pathogenesis to Targeted Therapy.
authors: Zhang T, Hu J, Sun M, Zhang X, Xu H, Du B, Wei Y, Wei R.
ai_summary: This review summarizes the biology of the S100A8/A9 heterodimer, a myeloid-cell-derived damage-associated molecular pattern that triggers cytokine, chemokine, and adhesion factor production upon receptor engagement. It describes how S100A8/A9 is upregulated and contributes to the pathogenesis of three autoimmune eye diseases—autoimmune uveitis, Sjögren's dry eye disease, and thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy—highlighting its potential as a diagnostic biomarker and discussing therapeutic strategies and future research directions for targeting S100A8/A9 in these ocular disorders.

title: The minor spliceosome component U4atac regulates JAK/STAT signaling to modulate hematopoiesis and immune responses in Drosophila melanogaster.
authors: Shikara D, Bishop E, Barton N, Makdissi S, Kailasam S, György A, Siekhaus DE, Borroto MC, Campeau PM, Vong L, Roifman CM, Parsons BD, Di Cara F.
ai_summary:
Gene: U4atac
Finding: A CRISPR/Cas9-induced Drosophila U4atac mutant in the conserved stem II region impairs splicing of innate immunity, hematopoiesis, and intestinal transcripts, reducing expression of the JAK homolog hopscotch and causing Hop-related hematopoietic defects; Jak1 expression and downstream signaling are likewise reduced in Roifman syndrome patients.
Disease: Roifman syndrome (RNU4atac-opathy)

title: Signaling pathways of inflammation in CIA model of rheumatoid arthritis regulated by cannabichromene.
authors: Sklenárová M, Šteigerová M, Jelínek P, Bazyuk M, Merdita S, Chaban B, Hlaváč J, Stránský D, Fučíková M, Šoóš M, Šíma M, Slanař O.
ai_summary:
Gene: STAT3
Finding: In a collagen-induced arthritis rat model, cannabichromene reduced arthritis scores and downregulated IL-6, STAT3, and IL-17A, indicating suppression of the TNF-NF-κB-IL-6-STAT3-Th17 axis, and also inhibited inflammasome components (NLRP3, NLRP1A, caspase-11), though it did not significantly reduce paw swelling or affect MMP-3/MMP-9.
Disease: Rheumatoid arthritis

title: The gut microbiota as a regulator of intestinal stem-cell fate: bacterial and fungal control of differentiation and regeneration.
authors: Shen Y, Chadwick BJ, Xue P, Gao Y, Ding C.
ai_summary: This review examines how bacterial and fungal signals regulate intestinal stem cell activity and epithelial repair via microbial metabolites, immune relays, and epithelial sensing. Bacterial metabolites and structural ligands act through Wnt/β-catenin, AHR, IL-22-STAT3, Hippo-YAP and related pathways, with effects varying by ligand, responding cell type, and tissue state. Evidence for fungi is more limited, with some fungal products engaging repair-associated pathways, but improved barrier function or reduced inflammation often observed without direct measurement of ISC fate. The authors propose a framework distinguishing direct changes in stem-cell self-renewal, lineage allocation, or regenerative state from indirect evidence based on epithelial repair, and identify key mechanistic gaps in how multi-kingdom microbial signals shape intestinal renewal.

title: Bioinformatics analysis of genes related to uveitis and differential gene expression in a model of experimental autoimmune uveitis.
authors: He K, Pan B, Tian P, Yang S.
ai_summary: This bioinformatics and experimental study identified 139 uveitis-related genes, enriched in inflammatory and immune responses and in TNF and NF-κB signaling, and narrowed these to ten hub genes (IL17A, IL18, TLR2, IL2, TLR4, IL10, IL1B, IL6, TNF, and CCL2), each with diagnostic potential (AUC > 0.6) in patient monocyte transcriptomes. In an IRBP-induced rat model of experimental autoimmune uveitis, the mRNA and protein levels of these hub genes were significantly elevated in ocular, liver, and spleen tissues alongside greater anterior segment inflammation, supporting their involvement in uveitis pathogenesis and their potential as diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

title: Fracture healing: from molecular and cellular mechanisms to therapeutic strategies.
authors: Staubli F, Ten Ham RMT, Bergsma JE, Gawlitta D, Man K.
ai_summary: This review synthesizes the molecular and cellular mechanisms governing fracture healing, a regenerative process requiring coordinated immune, vascular, neural, and skeletal signaling. It highlights key pathways—cytokine signaling, angiogenesis, mechanotransduction, hypoxia sensing, and osteochondral differentiation—whose disruption by injury, systemic disease, aging, or metabolic dysregulation leads to delayed union or nonunion. The authors critically evaluate emerging targeted therapies, including growth factors, anabolic and immunomodulatory agents, cell- and gene-based approaches, extracellular vesicles, and biomaterial-assisted delivery, assessing their biological rationale and translational limitations, and argue for shifting from descriptive pathology toward actionable signaling frameworks to guide next-generation bone regeneration therapies.

title: CaMKII-based gene therapy protects retinal ganglion cells in a broad range of disease: ischemic retinopathy and congenital glaucoma.
authors: Zhou J, Wan Y, Anderson MG, Duh EJ, Demb JB, Guo X, Chen B.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
ai_summary:
Gene: CaMKII
Finding: CaMKII-based gene therapy robustly protects retinal ganglion cells and preserves visual function in mouse models of ischemic injury and congenital glaucoma, suggesting CaMKII as a broad therapeutic target for retinal diseases driven by acute and chronic intraocular pressure elevation.
Disease: Ischemic retinopathy and congenital glaucoma

title: Emerging CAR-Treg and regulatory T cell therapies for inflammatory bowel diseases: a systematic review of a new era of treatment.
authors: Suarez-Trujillo F, Steiner TS, Gisbert JP, Chaparro M.
ai_summary: This systematic review of 11 preclinical, translational, and clinical studies evaluates CAR-Treg and regulatory T cell therapies for inflammatory bowel disease. CAR-Tregs extend conventional CAR-T technology to achieve antigen-specific immune regulation rather than cytotoxicity, and preclinical and early translational data support their biological plausibility and feasibility. However, human evidence remains sparse with short follow-up, and key unresolved issues include cellular persistence, Treg phenotypic stability, optimal antigen selection, manufacturing scalability, and long-term safety. The authors conclude these therapies remain investigational and require robust clinical trials with standardized endpoints and long-term safety monitoring before adoption.

title: Gut microbiota-innate immune crosstalk in the initiation and progression of CRC: mechanisms and therapeutic potential.
authors: Lin J, Lin H, Zhang Z, Wang H.
ai_summary: This review examines the bidirectional crosstalk between gut microbiota and innate immunity in colorectal cancer. Microbes influence Toll-like and NOD-like receptor signaling, NF-κB activation, the NLRP3 inflammasome, and immunometabolic pathways via structural components, metabolites, virulence factors, and outer membrane vesicles, remodeling macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and NK cells; innate immunity in turn shapes microbial composition and distribution through antimicrobial effectors, barrier maintenance, inflammatory mediators, and phagocytosis. These interactions are linked to immune surveillance changes, myeloid microenvironment alterations, barrier dysfunction, low-grade inflammation, tumor microenvironment remodeling, EMT-related phenotypes, and immune evasion. The authors stress that colibactin-associated mutational signatures in human CRC genomes are among the few high-strength mechanistic findings, while most specific microbiota-immune interactions rest on animal or in vitro evidence with limited longitudinal human causal data, and they call for cautious interpretation in developing precision interventions.

title: Microbiota-miR-101 interactions in obesity-associated colorectal cancer: from barrier dysfunction to precision therapeutic strategies.
authors: Mishra SP, Jacobson R, Wang B, Prajapati S, Sanberg P, Brechot C, Jain S, Yadav H.
ai_summary:
Gene: STAT3
Finding: Elevated dietary and microbiota-derived ethanolamine induces colonic epithelial miR-101a overexpression, which destabilizes ZO-1 (TJP1) mRNA to impair barrier integrity and drive chronic inflammation, activating pro-survival pathways including STAT3 and AKT that foster a tumor-permissive microenvironment.
Disease: Obesity-associated colorectal cancer

title: Phytocompounds with immunomodulatory activities: mechanisms, therapeutic potential, and clinical prospects.
authors: Mehana NA, Morad NI, Mekky R, Mahfoz AM, El-Shiekh RA, Elrebehy MA.
ai_summary: This review synthesizes evidence on plant-derived compounds (polysaccharides, flavonoids, polyphenols, terpenoids, and alkaloids) as immunomodulators, based on a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2000 and 2025. These phytocompounds act on innate and adaptive immune cells—macrophages, dendritic cells, T and B lymphocytes, and natural killer cells—and modulate signaling pathways including NF-κB, MAPKs, JAK/STAT, and Nrf2, giving them pleiotropic effects relevant to autoimmune diseases, chronic inflammation, infections, and immune-mediated metabolic disorders. The authors conclude that despite promising preclinical and clinical results, unresolved issues of safety, pharmacokinetics, standardized dosing, and lack of large-scale trials still limit therapeutic translation.

title: Therapeutic potential of ginseng and its bioactive compounds in inflammatory bowel disease: current evidence and future directions.
authors: Islam MM, Park IH, Kang KS.
ai_summary: This review summarizes preclinical evidence that ginseng and its bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides, may alleviate experimental colitis through multiple mechanisms—inhibiting inflammatory signaling pathways, regulating cytokine production, modulating immune cell activity, and altering the gut microbiota—positioning them as promising alternatives to conventional IBD therapies that carry inconsistent efficacy and adverse effects. However, clinical studies of ginsenosides in IBD remain extremely limited, and the authors outline current challenges and future directions for translating these findings.

title: Strain-resolved biology of Lactobacillus johnsonii across host systems.
authors: Li M, He J, Chai J, Deng F, Li Y.
ai_summary: This review argues that Lactobacillus johnsonii should be viewed as a strain-dependent, host-associated lineage rather than a uniform probiotic species. Synthesizing comparative genomic, mechanistic, and intervention studies—chiefly in weaned piglets, where barrier injury, inflammation, dysbiosis, diarrhea, and poor growth coincide—it shows that selected strains can reduce diarrhea and pathogen burden and improve barrier, immune, oxidative, and metabolic markers. Strain-level differences in surface architecture, adhesion, exopolysaccharides, redox activity, and extracellular vesicles underlie recurring mechanisms such as colonization resistance, epithelial barrier support, immune regulation, and stress control. The authors caution that the strongest evidence ties a named strain to a defined host context and measurable phenotype, whereas species-level abundance, multistrain formulations, and rodent models are weak bases for inferring efficacy in livestock.

title: Diverse bacterial pattern recognition receptors sense the core phage proteome.
authors: Lee H, Luengo-Woods S, Zhang J, Makarova KS, Wolf YI, Chiu C, Evans SA, Chen J, Xiao H, Feng L, Koonin EV, Gao A.
ai_summary: Bacteria and archaea use at least 90 structurally distinct STAND NTPase families for antiviral defence, far more than previously appreciated. The uncharacterized Avs7 family was shown to recognize the major capsid protein (MCP) of tailed phages; cryo-EM structures of Salmonella enterica Avs7 revealed an asymmetric butterfly-shaped tetramer that assembles stepwise via large MCP-induced conformational changes and incorporates elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) as a structural component that boosts defence. Genetic screens with a 687-phage-gene library showed that 13 additional STAND families sense 13 conserved phage proteins covering most core structural and replicative components of tailed phages, including two further MCP sensors (Avs8, Avs10) and Avs11–21, which detect the portal, portal adaptor, tail nozzle, head–tail connector, tail terminator, tail tube protein, tail assembly chaperone, tape measure protein, DNA polymerase, helicase/RecA-type ATPase and single-stranded DNA annealing protein. The work establishes structure-based pattern recognition of the core phage proteome, via repurposing of host factors, as a fundamental strategy of bacterial immunity.

title: Baicalein Attenuates Eosinophilic Rhinosinusitis by Suppressing ALOX15-Mediated M2 Macrophage Function.
authors: Wang L, Zhu Z, Liu Y, Aodeng S, Kang T, Wang W, Lv W.
ai_summary:
Gene: ALOX15
Finding: Baicalein attenuated eosinophilic rhinosinusitis in a papain-induced mouse model by suppressing ALOX15-mediated lipid peroxidation and M2 macrophage secretory function, with the ALOX15 inhibitor PD146176 producing similar effects and no additive effect when combined with baicalein.
Disease: Eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (eCRSwNP)

title: Evaluation of Stathmin Expression in Different Oral Squamous Lesions: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: Zare R, Esmailizadeh P, Amirmoezi F.
ai_summary: Stathmin expression was compared across 98 oral mucosal samples spanning benign hyperkeratosis, lichen planus with and without dysplasia, epithelial dysplasia, and oral squamous cell carcinoma. Expression in the central/suprabasal epithelial layer was significantly higher in OSCC than lichen planus, and higher in epithelial dysplasia and lichen planus with dysplasia than in hyperkeratosis or lichen planus without dysplasia. The authors conclude stathmin is upregulated in lesions with dysplastic features and propose it as a potential marker of dysplasia in oral squamous lesions, with its signaling pathway and inhibitors as possible therapeutic targets.

title: AMOTL2 inhibits lymph node metastasis in gastric cancer by suppressing TGF-β/Smad signaling and is destabilized by the E3 ubiquitin ligase SMURF1.
authors: Wang H, Yang B, Lin C, Wang Y, Lu Y, Li J, Li J, Yu K, Wang M, Liu P, Wang Y, Li Y.
ai_summary:
Gene: AMOTL2
Finding: AMOTL2 is downregulated in gastric cancer, suppresses proliferation, migration, invasion, angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis by inhibiting TGF-β/Smad signaling, and is ubiquitinated and degraded by the E3 ligase SMURF1, which binds it via its WW domains.
Disease: Gastric cancer (tumor progression and lymph node metastasis)

title: Structural Model of the Oncostatin M (OSM)-OSMRβ-gp130 Ternary Complex Reveals Pathways of Allosteric Communication in OSM Signaling.
authors: Du Q, Luo D, Xue W, Qian Y.
ai_summary: A full-length structural model of the human OSM–OSMRβ–gp130 ternary complex was built using AlphaFold2 and all-atom molecular dynamics simulation, revealing that OSM binding induces structural rearrangements in the heterodimeric receptors that propagate signals from the extracellular to the intracellular domains. Two main allosteric pathways were identified linking the allosteric region of OSM to the active sites of OSMRβ and gp130, and two druggable binding sites on OSM and gp130 were detected, offering targets for small-molecule inhibition of OSM signaling in inflammatory diseases and cancer.

title: Does acute inflammation triggered by infection promote cancer progression?
authors: Valença-Pereira F, Johnson B, DeGregori J, Rincon M.
ai_summary: Acute infections with common respiratory viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 have been implicated in cancer progression, with experimental evidence that infection-driven inflammation can promote tumor expansion and dissemination. The acute inflammatory cascade and dynamic immune cell reprogramming rapidly remodel the tissue microenvironment to favor cancer cell survival, growth, and immune evasion, though acute infections can also elicit anti-tumor immune responses. Understanding how infections differentially skew immune programs to promote or restrain cancer progression will be essential for developing future therapeutic strategies.

title: Chemistry and Biological Activity of 11H-Indeno[1,2-b]quinoxalin-11-ones and Tryptanthrins, Their Oximes, and Related Analogues.
authors: Schepetkin IA, Plotnikov MB, Kovrizhina AR, Khlebnikov AI.
ai_summary: This review covers the synthesis, stereochemistry, and biological activity of tetracyclic ketoximes derived from 11H-indeno[1,2-b]quinoxalin-11-one and the natural alkaloid tryptanthrin. Converting their exocyclic carbonyls to oximes modulates frontier orbital energies, adds chelating pharmacophores, and enables nitric oxide release; modern microwave, sonochemical, photocatalytic, and multicomponent methods give efficient access to these compounds, and crystallography, spectroscopy, and DFT establish a thermodynamic preference for the E-oxime configuration. The oximes bind JNK1-3 with high affinity, underlying neuroprotective effects in cerebral ischemia and Alzheimer-like models, dual JNK inhibition plus NO-mediated cardioprotection in hypertension and myocardial infarction, and anti-inflammatory action via NF-κB/AP-1 suppression, with additional anticancer, antimicrobial, antiviral, and antidiabetic activities attributed to DNA intercalation, topoisomerase inhibition, metal coordination, and kinase blockade. Despite compelling preclinical profiles, poor oral bioavailability and rapid hepatic clearance remain major obstacles, prompting work on formulations, prodrugs, and structure-activity optimization.

title: Extrinsic Regulation of Optic Nerve Axon Regeneration in the Adult Central Nervous System.
authors: Adhikary A, Dorairaj E, Arshavsky A, Ramcharan S, Kishor KS, Bhattacharya SK.
ai_summary: This review argues that failed optic nerve regeneration in the adult CNS cannot be explained by limited intrinsic neuronal growth capacity alone; the extrinsic environment is the dominant determinant. It reframes the optic nerve environment as a dynamic "regenerative niche" in which vascular, immune, glial, matrix, and metabolic compartments are spatially co-localized and temporally coordinated rather than independent barriers. These compartments share a trajectory—broadly protective acutely, then inhibitory once the response fails to resolve—and actively drive one another (e.g., reactive astrocytes promote matrix remodeling that later restricts regrowth). Overall permissiveness therefore reflects the aggregate, interdependent state of the niche, not any single barrier. The review synthesizes evidence on extrinsic barriers, intervention opportunities, and disease-specific variability relevant to retinal ganglion cell axon regeneration, concluding that interventions must account for spatial, temporal, and metabolic factors to achieve functional recovery and vision restoration.

title: Patient-matched transcriptomics of in vivo and in vitro colonic epithelium substantiate organoids as a translational model for ulcerative colitis.
authors: Walaas GAE, Sridhar A, Kuraas LF, Sæterstad S, Schioldborg AY, Van Beelen Granlund A, Sandvik AK, Østvik AE, Bakke I, Bruland T.
ai_summary: Cytokine-stimulated intestinal epithelial organoids derived from ulcerative colitis (UC) patients recapitulate key features of in vivo epithelial inflammation, including interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and unfolded protein response pathways. Comparing patient-matched laser-microdissected colonic epithelium with organoids from the same donors showed that TNF + IFNγ and a multi-cytokine cocktail most closely matched the inflamed epithelial state, with concordance across over 350 UC-relevant genes and protein-level confirmation of IRF1, ERAP2, NOS2, and DUOX2. These findings support cytokine-stimulated organoids as a personalized translational model for studying epithelial-specific disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets in UC.

title: Microencapsulation of a novel Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron strain: a promising strategy to fortify intestinal barrier fortification in a weaned pig model.
authors: Jin S, Liu Y, Zhang Y, Shen Y, Lan C, Li H, He J, Wu A, Tang J, Zhang R, Wang H, Wang Q, Tian G, Cai J, Mao X, Good EL, Luo Y.
ai_summary: Microencapsulation of the porcine probiotic strain Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron LYH5 was optimized using sodium alginate and gellan gum, achieving an 84.22% encapsulation rate. In a 40-day trial with 78 weaned piglets, dietary supplementation with LYH5 microcapsules improved intestinal barrier function without affecting growth performance, whereas the strain alone showed poor gastric juice tolerance. The work presents microencapsulation as a strategy to overcome gastric acid sensitivity and support probiotic development.

title: The Impact of Peptidoglycan Structure on Immune Sensing.
authors: Cardozo S, Skerry C.
ai_summary: This review examines how the structural diversity of peptidoglycan (PGN) and its released muropeptide fragments determines host immune recognition. It describes how structurally distinct muropeptides are synthesized and processed, and how they are selectively sensed by host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). The authors emphasize that PGN is recognized not only through canonical di-/tripeptides but also through novel structural motifs, and that differential immune recognition shapes PRR activation, host-pathogen interactions, and infection outcomes. The mechanisms underlying recognition of these diverse fragments and their roles in immune activation, pathogenesis, and immune evasion remain poorly understood.

title: Polo-like kinase phosphorylation of the orphan kinesin KIN-G negatively regulates centrin arm biogenesis in Trypanosoma brucei.
authors: Kurasawa Y, Zhou Q, Lee KJ, Hu H, Li Z.
ai_summary:
Gene: KIN-G
Finding: TbPLK phosphorylates KIN-G at multiple residues including Thr301 within a microtubule-binding motif, inhibiting its microtubule-binding activity and negatively regulating centrin arm biogenesis; a Thr301 phospho-mimic disrupts centrin arm integrity, Golgi duplication, flagellum attachment zone elongation, flagellum positioning, and cell division plane placement.
Disease: Centrin arm biogenesis defects in Trypanosoma brucei (flagellum-associated cytoskeletal duplication and cell division phenotypes)

title: Restoring neuroplasticity after CNS trauma: cell therapy approaches in spinal cord and traumatic brain injury.
authors: Palha AT, Lima MF, Carvalho M, Campos J, Sampaio-Marques B, Salgado AJ.
ai_summary: This review examines cell-based and cell-free therapies aimed at restoring neuroplasticity after spinal cord injury (SCI) and traumatic brain injury (TBI), where limited CNS regeneration, inflammation, and an inhibitory microenvironment impair recovery. It surveys candidate cell types—bone marrow-, adipose-, and umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells, neural progenitor cells, and olfactory ensheathing cells—and notes that clinical SCI studies report functional improvements, particularly with BMSCs and peripheral blood-derived stem cells, though methodological heterogeneity prevents firm conclusions. Clinical evidence in TBI is more limited, while preclinical work consistently shows neuroprotective and regenerative effects of mesenchymal stem cell therapies. Cell-free approaches using secretomes and extracellular vesicles may reproduce benefits while avoiding safety and logistical issues. The authors conclude that both strategies hold promise for enhancing neuroplasticity and functional recovery, but translation requires larger controlled trials and standardized protocols for timing, dosage, and administration route.

title: Gut microbiota-immune-metabolic crosstalk in acute lung injury: integrating the gut-lung axis from mechanism to therapeutic targeting.
authors: Wu W, Wang Z, Li Y, Luo N, Chen R, Zeng R, Li J.
ai_summary: This review examines how the gut-lung axis contributes to acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In critical illness, loss of intestinal barrier integrity and microbial imbalance allow bacteria, endotoxins, and metabolites to enter the circulation, driving pulmonary inflammation and immune dysregulation. Microbiota-derived metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives shape immune cell differentiation, particularly the balance between regulatory T cells and Th17 cells, while gut- and bone-marrow-derived immune cells also influence pulmonary immunity; communication is bidirectional, as lung microbiota changes can affect intestinal homeostasis. The authors discuss therapeutic strategies targeting this axis, including microbiota modulation, fecal microbiota transplantation, and metabolic interventions, as potential approaches for preventing and treating ALI/ARDS in critical care.

title: Engineering Small Extracellular Vesicles for Colon-Targeted Delivery: Microenvironment-Responsive Design, Therapeutic Mechanisms, and Clinical Translation.
authors: Liu G, Li M, Liu J, Li YP, Huang X, Guo X, Zhai Q, Zhang F, Yan W, Sun J.
ai_summary: This review examines engineered small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) as colon-targeted drug delivery vehicles, comparing them with conventional systems and covering their biogenesis, cargo loading, isolation, characterization, and surface engineering. It details passive, active, and stimuli-responsive targeting strategies that exploit colon-specific cues such as distal gastrointestinal pH, microbiota-derived enzymes, inflammatory reactive oxygen species, and lesion-associated receptors (integrins, CD44, folate receptors), while addressing the need to survive gastric acidity and proteolysis and to cross the mucus barrier. Therapeutic applications are assessed in inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer—including epithelial barrier restoration, immune regulation, macrophage polarization, apoptosis, and tumor-microenvironment remodeling—as well as emerging indications like irritable bowel syndrome. The authors also discuss clinical trials, Good Manufacturing Practice requirements, potency and release specifications, safety, and regulatory uncertainties, and propose a disease- and route-oriented decision framework linking cargo properties, administration route, target-cell biology, manufacturing feasibility, and clinical endpoints. Although no engineered sEV therapeutic has achieved full regulatory approval, the review argues that microfluidic manufacturing, organ-on-chip validation, AI-assisted design, and image-guided delivery could improve reproducibility and translational readiness.

title: Cough hypersensitivity risk increases during heatwaves and can be reduced by inhalation of alkaline aerosols of endogenous ions.
authors: Button B, Edwards A, Chung KF, Dang H, Gutay M, Griffin N, Gerenza J, Wang L, Abubakar-Waziri H, Bhatta DB, Ausiello DA, Li D, Alotaibi B, Altassan KK, Edwards DA.
ai_summary: Heatwave exposure (35 °C, 30% relative humidity) caused upper-airway mucosal collapse in human bronchial epithelial cell cultures and elevated cough hypersensitivity risk in human clinical studies. Inhalation of alkaline hypertonic divalent salt (HDS) aerosols reversed this effect, suggesting a protective strategy for respiratory health under global warming.

title: Semaglutide and pioglitazone restore airway mucosal homeostasis by resolving Pseudomonas aeruginosa pyocyanin-induced mucus hypersecretion, ciliostasis, and type 2 airway inflammation.
authors: Wu C, Kulkarni NA, Lew SQ, Choi W, Sivaguru M, Kosmider B, Nanjappa SG, Lau GW.
ai_summary: Semaglutide (a GLP-1R agonist) and pioglitazone (a PPARγ agonist) were the most effective of the tested agonists at reducing pyocyanin-induced MUC5AC mucin expression and ROS production in 16HBE14o- cells and in mouse lungs, and at restoring mucociliary beat frequency and transport in air-liquid interface cultures of primary human small airway epithelial cells. Their protective effects were partially reversed by the GLP1R antagonist Exendin(9-39) and the PPARγ antagonist GW9662, confirming GLP1R/PPARγ-dependent mechanisms. Both drugs also attenuated type 2 immune responses and neutrophil influx and reduced P. aeruginosa burden in a mouse chronic bronchitis infection model, suggesting a repurposing opportunity for COPD.

title: E3 Ubiquitin Ligases in Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
authors: Wang S, Pan X, Zhang K, Zhao D, Chen X, Wang Y, Hu H, Zhang Y.
ai_summary: This review synthesizes genetic and functional evidence linking E3 ubiquitin ligases and their associated complexes to neurodevelopmental disorders. Enrichment and mechanistic analyses indicate that these genes converge on early neurodevelopment, neuronal migration, synaptic and circuit maturation, proteostasis, metabolism, and intracellular trafficking. Evidence strength varies: UBE3A-related Angelman syndrome is the clearest example of mechanism-guided therapy (UBE3A restoration, paternal allele reactivation), whereas most non-UBE3A mechanisms remain at the stage of pathway analysis, preclinical modulation, or candidate substrate validation. The authors call for clarifying variant-specific effects, defining direct disease-relevant substrates, and establishing reproducible readouts for mechanism-based therapeutic development.

title: Viscotaxis: An Emerging Driver for Directed Cell Migration.
authors: Chen Z, Wang Z, Wang G.
ai_summary: This mini-review defines viscotaxis—directed cell migration along gradients of extracellular fluid viscosity or matrix loss modulus—and distinguishes it from the related but physically distinct cues of substrate stiffness, matrix viscoelasticity, and stress relaxation, with which it is often conflated. It surveys the physiological and pathological relevance of viscotaxis across development, tissue homeostasis, immunity, and cancer, and outlines a putative multi-step mechanosensory cascade underlying viscotactic responses. The authors examine how viscotaxis may synergize or compete with durotaxis, haptotaxis, chemotaxis, electrotaxis, and phototaxis under mixed microenvironmental cues, and compare proposed hydrodynamic versus steric-exclusion mechanisms across spiral microbes, flagellated eukaryotes, mammalian cells, and embryonic tissues. They emphasize that biological functions and molecular underpinnings remain largely uncharacterized and that direct evidence in mammalian systems is limited to a small number of studies, explicitly separating evidence from viscosity gradients versus uniformly elevated viscosity and established findings from working hypotheses. The review concludes by discussing methodological bottlenecks and unresolved conceptual debates and proposing biomaterial tools and therapeutic strategies to advance viscotaxis from a biophysical curiosity toward a core principle of cellular mechanobiology.

title: Orchestrating brain fluid dynamics: circadian regulation of CSF, glymphatic exchange, and waste clearance.
authors: Ciampi C, Govoni S, Preda S, Di Cesare Mannelli L, Racchi M, Martelli A, Lanni C.
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
ai_summary: This review synthesizes literature on how circadian biological clocks regulate cerebrospinal fluid production and glymphatic exchange, proposing an integrated model in which clocks operating at multiple levels of the CSF/interstitial fluid/glymphatic chain coordinate fluid dynamics. Central to this model is the neurovascular unit, which governs fluidic control and exchange at the neuron/astrocyte/endothelium interface. While animal studies increasingly support daily cycling of glymphatic waste clearance, the precise coordination and primary location of the underlying clocks remain unresolved. The authors argue that understanding this circadian orchestration is essential for comprehending brain homeostasis and disease, and they call for further research into the localization and function of these clocks.

title: Cellular Responses to Mechanical Cues Across Scales: From Fundamental Insights to Translational Potential.
authors: Polz M, Kainz MP, Haider N, Rienmüller T, Lenk K, Kargl R, Terzano M, Sommer G, Holzapfel GA, Fuchs J.
ai_summary: This review proposes a framework for judging how well mechanobiology findings translate across biological scales, from single cells and organoids to tissues and organs. It first standardizes terminology by categorizing soft biomaterials according to their architecture and mechanical properties, then examines how cells interpret mechanical signals in advanced in vitro systems that mimic physiological mechanical environments. Using a scoring system and comparative analysis, the authors argue that physiological specificity, rather than experimental complexity, determines predictive value: simple systems can be highly translatable when their mechanical cues match native conditions, whereas advanced models need careful validation. Integrating biomechanics, electrophysiology, and systems biology, the review outlines principles and validation strategies to improve the predictive utility of mechanobiological findings and guide the design of better biomaterials and tissue-engineered systems.

title: Tearing Down Scientific Boundaries: Frontiers in Medicinal Chemistry 2026.
authors: Heitel P, Barbie P, Gambardella A, Pinto M, Pape F, Tarasewicz A, Hessler G, Wünsch B, Schiedel M, Lamers C.
ai_summary: This is a conference report describing the Frontiers in Medicinal Chemistry 2026 meeting held in Münster, which drew over 240 participants from about 20 countries and featured more than 40 lectures and 125 posters. The authors, from the NextGenMedChem group, summarize their highlights from the event. It contains no gene, experimental finding, or disease link.
